953.title: The tablecloth
953.hook: Moses Isserles of Kraków adds Ashkenazi customs, called "the tablecloth"
953.howItsDone: Printed editions of the Shulchan Aruch include Isserles's notes inside Karo's text, and Ashkenazi Jews generally follow his rulings where they differ from Karo's, while Sephardic communities generally follow Karo.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shulchan Aruch, Joseph Karo's code written in Tzfat. Your line was the set table. Did you set one on purpose? Today, the table travels north, and someone adds a cloth. Day nine hundred fifty-three.

Passover in Kraków. On one family's table, there is no rice, no beans, no lentils, though nothing in the Torah forbids them. Far to the south, in Tzfat or Salonika, a Sephardic family may well be eating rice at the same seder. Both are keeping Passover. Both are following their parents. So when a code of law arrives from Tzfat and says what Jews do, a rabbi in Kraków has a problem: whose practice does the book describe? His answer was not to throw the book away. It was to spread something over it. Today, the tablecloth.
screen: `TWO SEDER TABLES.` → `RICE ON ONE, NOT THE OTHER.` → `WHOSE PRACTICE IS IN THE BOOK?`

segments.voice: The rabbi was Moses Isserles of Kraków, known by his initials as the Rema. He had been working on his own long study of the same laws Karo had studied. When the Shulchan Aruch appeared, he did not write a rival code. He wrote notes on it. Wherever the customs of Ashkenaz, the Jews of Germany and Poland, differed from Karo's ruling, he added a short comment: this is our practice. He called those notes the Mappah, which means the tablecloth. The joke is gentle and exact. Karo had set the table; Isserles spread a cloth over it, so it could be used in another house. Printers later set his notes right inside Karo's text, in a different typeface, so one page held both. So the book that Sephardic and Ashkenazic Jews both use is a shared page with two voices on it, neither erasing the other. Behind the Mappah is a high respect for minhag, custom. Isserles treated the practices of a community, handed down from parents, as something that carries weight in law, not as an afterthought. Proverbs puts it simply: "forsake not the teaching of thy mother." Some readers have heard custom in that line, the things learned at home before anyone opened a book. So when you see a Jewish practice done one way in one family and another way next door, it may be neither mistake nor laziness. It may be the set table and the tablecloth, side by side.
screen: `ISSERLES OF KRAKÓW, THE REMA.` · `NOTES, NOT A RIVAL CODE.` · `ONE PAGE, TWO VOICES.` · then, large: `THE TEACHING OF THY MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: honor a custom not your own. Settle your breath. Bring to mind a practice from someone else's family or community that you don't share: a holiday food, a way of greeting, a quiet ritual before a meal, the way they mourn or celebrate. Instead of asking whether it's right, ask what it holds for them. Whose hands taught it? What does it remember? Let that respect sit beside your own way of doing things. The bell holds the time.
The tablecloth. The Mappah, Moses Isserles's notes on the Shulchan Aruch, adding Ashkenazi custom so that one book could serve more than one community. Today's word.
Your line: the tablecloth. Today, when someone does a thing differently from you, ask them where their way comes from, and listen to the answer. Day nine hundred fifty-three.

954.title: The Ari
954.hook: Isaac Luria teaches in Safed for about two years and transforms Jewish mystical thought
954.howItsDone: Some Jews study the Ari's teachings in Kabbalah circles, and some prayer books, especially in Hasidic and Sephardic communities, follow customs and intentions drawn from his school.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mappah, Moses Isserles's notes on Karo's code. Your line was the tablecloth. Whose custom did you ask about? Today, back to Tzfat, and a teacher who wrote almost nothing down. Day nine hundred fifty-four.

How long does it take to change the way a people prays? A lifetime, perhaps. A great book, a school, a long career. Here is a teacher who, tradition says, spent only a short time in Tzfat before he died young. He wrote very little. He taught a small circle of students, out loud, on walks and at tables. And yet the ideas they carried away shaped Jewish prayer books and mystical study, and some hear them in a phrase about fixing the world. Today, the Ari.
screen: `A SHORT TIME IN TZFAT.` → `ALMOST NOTHING WRITTEN.` → `IDEAS THAT TRAVELED FAR.`

segments.voice: His name was Rabbi Isaac Luria. Ari means lion in Hebrew, and tradition says the title also stands for the initials of a phrase meaning the godly Rabbi Isaac. His teachings come to us mainly through a student, Chaim Vital, who wrote them down in a large work called Etz Chaim, the Tree of Life. The heart of what the Ari taught is a story about creation, told in three movements. First, tzimtzum, contraction. How can there be a world at all, if God is everywhere? The Ari taught that God, as it were, drew back, making room. Second, the breaking of the vessels. Divine light poured into vessels that could not hold it, and they shattered. Sparks of holiness fell and were scattered through the world, hidden in ordinary things. Third, tikkun, repair. In this teaching, every prayer said with intention, every commandment done with care, lifts a spark and helps mend what broke. Some historians, Gershom Scholem among them, see in it a story that matched the lives of the exiles from Spain: a world cracked open, holiness scattered like a people, and a task for each person to help put it back together. It turned small acts into large ones. The phrase tikkun olam, repairing the world, is older than the Ari: it appears in the Mishnah and in the Aleinu prayer. But since his time it can carry an echo of this teaching. A psalm asks for exactly the wisdom of a short life: "So teach us to number our days, that we may get us a heart of wisdom." The lion taught briefly. The roar carried.
screen: `LURIA, THE LION.` · `GOD DRAWS BACK: TZIMTZUM.` · `THE VESSELS BREAK.` · then, large: `TIKKUN: REPAIR.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: learn from something brief. Settle and breathe. Call to mind something short that changed you: a sentence a teacher once said, a summer job, a friend you knew for only a few months, a single conversation with a stranger. Hold it lightly. What did it leave you with that you still carry? Let the shortness of it sit beside the size of what it gave. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: teach us to number our days. The bell holds the time.
The Ari. Rabbi Isaac Luria of Tzfat, the lion, who taught contraction, the breaking of the vessels, and repair, and whose students carried those ideas into Jewish prayer and thought. Today's word.
Your line: the lion. Today, do one small thing with full attention, as if it were lifting a hidden spark. Day nine hundred fifty-four.

955.title: Walking out to greet Shabbat
955.hook: the Safed mystics walk into the fields on Friday to meet Shabbat
955.howItsDone: On Friday evening, Jewish congregations sing Kabbalat Shabbat, including Lecha Dodi, and at its last verse the congregation often turns to face the door to welcome Shabbat as a bride.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ari, Isaac Luria, and the sparks waiting to be lifted. Your line was the lion. What small thing did you do with full attention? Today, the Ari's town on a Friday afternoon. Day nine hundred fifty-five.

Friday, late afternoon, on the edge of Tzfat. The cooking is done. The lamps are ready. And instead of waiting indoors, a group of men walk out of town, down the slope, into the fields. They face west, toward the setting sun, and begin to sing. They are not going anywhere. They are going out to meet someone. Tradition says the mystics of Tzfat did this week after week, as if the guest they were greeting were coming up the road. Today, walking out to greet Shabbat.
screen: `FRIDAY, LATE AFTERNOON.` → `OUT INTO THE FIELDS.` → `FACING THE SETTING SUN.`

segments.voice: The idea is older than Tzfat. The Talmud tells of two sages and their Friday habits. Rabbi Hanina would wrap himself in his cloak as the sun went down and say: come, let us go out to greet Shabbat the queen. Rabbi Yannai would put on his Shabbat clothes and say: come, O bride, come, O bride. Shabbat, in their words, is not just a day that arrives. She is someone you go out to meet. The mystics of Tzfat took those words literally and walked into the fields. Out of that circle came a poem, Lecha Dodi, written by Shlomo Halevi Alkabetz. Its refrain says, in Hebrew, lecha dodi likrat kallah: come, my beloved, to meet the bride. Look closely at the Hebrew: the first letters of its opening verses spell out the poet's name. The Friday evening psalms that welcome Shabbat in the synagogue, called Kabbalat Shabbat, grew from this same setting, and they lead into the psalm the Bible titles for the day. It begins: "A Psalm, a Song. For the sabbath day." Today the fields have mostly turned into a doorway. When the last verse of Lecha Dodi is sung, congregations often turn around to face the synagogue door and bow, as though the bride were walking in. It's a small movement. But it keeps the old walk alive: Shabbat is still greeted, not just noticed.
screen: `HANINA AND YANNAI GO OUT TO MEET HER.` · `THE MYSTICS WALK INTO THE FIELDS.` · `LECHA DODI: COME, MY BELOVED.` · then, large: `TURNING TO THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: greet Shabbat outdoors. If you can, step outside, or stand at a window that faces west. If it's not Friday, greet the evening instead, or simply the next rest you'll have. Let the light on the buildings and the sky be what you watch. Notice the change in it, slow and certain. Instead of waiting for rest to find you, turn toward it. If you pray, you can whisper the old words: come, O bride. The bell holds the time.
Walking out to greet Shabbat. Going out to meet the day of rest like a bride or a queen, as the Talmud's sages did and the mystics of Tzfat did in the fields. Today's word.
screen: `WALKING OUT TO GREET SHABBAT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: walk out to meet her. Today, when your next rest comes, go to meet it: step outside, stand up, turn toward it, instead of letting it slip in unnoticed. Day nine hundred fifty-five.

956.title: The ghetto
956.hook: Venice walls in its Jews in 1516, the first ghetto
956.howItsDone: The old ghetto of Venice still has working synagogues and a Jewish museum, and Jews visiting the city often go to pray or remember there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mystics of Tzfat walking into the fields on Friday. Your line was walk out to meet her. Did you turn toward your rest? Today, a place where walking out was locked at night. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

The guard at the gate is paid by the people he locks in. Each evening in Venice, as bells ring across the water, he swings a heavy gate shut on one small island in the city. Behind it, Jewish families settle in for the night. They may go out by day to trade, to work, to see a patient. After dark, by law, they must be inside. In the morning the gate opens again. Across the canal, the rest of the city goes about its evening. Today, the ghetto.
screen: `A GATE SWINGS SHUT.` → `INSIDE BY NIGHTFALL.` → `OPEN AGAIN AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: The Republic of Venice allowed Jews to live in the city, but only in one enclosed area. Some say the name ghetto comes from a foundry that once stood there; whatever its source, the word stuck, and it later spread to enclosed Jewish quarters in other cities. The rules were simple and hard. Gates locked at night. Guards at the gates, paid, as we heard, by the Jews themselves. Jews needed permission to live in Venice at all, and the permission had to be renewed. Because the area could not grow outward, the buildings grew upward, story on story, crowded and tall. And yet look inside the walls. Synagogues were tucked into the upper floors of ordinary buildings, so that from the street you might never know they were there. Different communities kept their own: Jews from Germany, from Italy, from Spain and Portugal and the East, each with its own melody and custom, side by side in a few crowded streets. Printers in Venice produced Hebrew books. Scholars taught and preached. Life went on, behind a gate. The Psalms have a blessing for walls: "Peace be within thy walls." The psalm means the walls of Jerusalem, walls that protect. The ghetto's walls were built by others, to keep a people apart. Both are true of this place: a cage from outside, and inside, a home that people made anyway. The word ghetto would later be used for far darker places. That is part of why today's line is said plainly: walls around people.
screen: `ONE ENCLOSED AREA.` · `GATES, GUARDS AND PERMITS.` · `SYNAGOGUES ON THE UPPER FLOORS.` · then, large: `PEACE BE WITHIN THY WALLS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: think of walls built around people. Breathe slowly. Bring to mind any wall you know of, real or invisible, that keeps a group of people apart: a fence, a rule, a neighborhood line, a door that only some can open. Don't argue with it yet. Just see the people on the other side, going about their evening, making a home inside it. Then see the faces of the ones who built it. Hold both in view while the bell holds the time.
The ghetto. The walled Jewish quarter of Venice, gated at night, where Jews were kept apart and still built synagogues, printing and a life of their own. Today's word.
Your line: walls around people. Today, notice one wall, a rule, a line, a closed door, and ask who it keeps apart and who built it. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

957.title: Amsterdam
957.hook: Spanish and Portuguese Jews rebuild open Jewish life in Amsterdam
957.howItsDone: Spanish and Portuguese Jewish congregations, including in Amsterdam, keep their own melodies and customs, and their members often tell the story of ancestors who returned to open Jewish life after living in secret.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ghetto in Venice. Your line was walls around people. Did you notice a wall today, built or invisible? Now we travel north, to a city of canals where the walls came down. Day nine hundred fifty-seven.

A grown man sits at a table with a teacher half his age, sounding out Hebrew letters like a child. His family has carried a secret for generations: clean linen laid on the beds every Friday, a grandmother who refused pork without ever saying why. Back in Portugal, saying more could have cost them everything. Here, in a port city of canals and warehouses, he can say it out loud. He is a Jew. Now he has to learn what that means. Today, the city where he learns it.
screen: `A GROWN MAN LEARNING HIS LETTERS.` → `A FAMILY SECRET.` → `NOW HE CAN SAY IT OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: After the expulsions from Spain and Portugal, some Jewish families stayed and were baptized, by force or under heavy pressure. Some of them kept Jewish customs in secret, and the Inquisition hunted for exactly those signs. Over time, some of these families slipped away, and a number of them reached Amsterdam, a trading city where they could live openly as Jews. Getting out was dangerous. Arriving brought a different problem: much had been forgotten. Some had never seen a Torah scroll or heard the prayers in Hebrew. So the newcomers set to work. They rebuilt Jewish life almost from the ground up. They brought in rabbis and teachers from other communities. They founded congregations and schools. Grown men chose to be circumcised. Prayer books and teachings were printed in Spanish and Portuguese, the languages people actually spoke, so they could find their way back. They called themselves a nation, and they governed their community with care, with elders who set rules and kept the peace. There is an old letter in the Tanakh that fits them. The prophet Jeremiah writes to Jews carried off to Babylon, far from home, and tells them not to wait with their bags packed: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them." Plant gardens. Raise families. Seek the peace of the city where you live. Amsterdam is that letter lived out. A new home, built on purpose. And an old faith, rebuilt piece by piece, by people who had nearly lost it and decided to learn it again.
screen: `BAPTIZED, BUT KEEPING SECRETS.` · `A CITY WHERE THEY COULD BE OPEN.` · `RELEARNING ALMOST EVERYTHING.` · `BUILD YE HOUSES, AND DWELL IN THEM.` · then, large: `NEW HOME, OLD FAITH.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: rebuild one thing. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Think of something you once had and let slip. A habit of prayer or quiet. A friendship. A language you used to speak. A song your family sang. Don't judge how it slipped away. Just hold it for a moment. Then ask: what is one small piece of it I could pick up again this week? One letter, one phone call, one verse. If you pray, you can ask for help in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Amsterdam. The trading city where Spanish and Portuguese Jews, some returning from secret lives, rebuilt open Jewish life. Today's word.
Your line: new home, old faith. Today, take one step toward something you let slip: one call, one page, one old song. Day nine hundred fifty-seven.

958.title: Spinoza
958.hook: a philosopher put under a ban by Amsterdam's Jewish community, argued about ever since
958.howItsDone: Spinoza's writings are studied in universities and argued over in Jewish schools of thought; some Jews regard the ban as justified, and others have asked for it to be reconsidered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amsterdam, where people rebuilt a faith they had nearly lost. Your line was new home, old faith. Did you pick up one thing you'd let slip? Today, a son of that same community who walked another way. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

In a small rented room, a man bends over a wheel, grinding glass into lenses. It is careful, quiet work: turn, polish, check against the light. In the evenings he writes, slowly, in Latin, building an argument the way he builds a lens, one exact surface at a time. Behind him, in Amsterdam, is the synagogue where he once studied as a boy. He no longer goes there. He can't. His own community has formally cut him off. Today, his name.
screen: `A MAN GRINDING LENSES.` → `WRITING IN LATIN AT NIGHT.` → `CUT OFF FROM HIS COMMUNITY.`

segments.voice: Baruch Spinoza grew up inside the Amsterdam community we met yesterday, the Portuguese Jews who had worked so hard to rebuild. He studied in its schools and knew its texts. As a young man he was placed under a ban by the community's leaders, and the ban's own text speaks of evil opinions and acts without naming them. His later books show the kind of questions he asked: who wrote the Torah, whether God chooses and commands as a person does, whether scripture should be read like any other old book. The ban was a cherem. A cherem cuts a person off: members were told not to speak with him or come near him, or read what he wrote. Remember who those leaders were. A community of former secret Jews, newly rebuilt, under the eyes of a Christian city that had taken them in. Some historians think they feared that his ideas put everyone at risk. Others think the ideas alone were enough. Spinoza did not join another religion. He lived quietly elsewhere in Holland and wrote. His books argued that God and nature are one reality, and that the Bible should be studied with the same tools as any text. And the story did not end with the ban. People have never stopped arguing about him. Some Jews see him as someone who left, and say the ban stands for good reason. Others claim him as a forerunner of modern Jewish thought, and have asked for the ban to be revisited. Philosophers argue too: some readers call him a man who denied God, while a German poet called him a God-intoxicated man. The same pages, read in opposite ways.
screen: `A SON OF THE AMSTERDAM COMMUNITY.` · `QUESTIONS THE LEADERS COULD NOT ACCEPT.` · `THE CHEREM: CUT OFF.` · `READ IN OPPOSITE WAYS.` · then, large: `ARGUED ABOUT EVER SINCE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: think one question through yourself. Sit and let your breathing slow. Pick one real question you carry, about God, or about how to live, or about something you were taught. Don't reach for the answer someone gave you, and don't reach for the opposite either. Just take one step at a time. What do I actually know here? What am I guessing? Where does my thinking stop? Let the question stay open if it needs to. If you pray, you can bring the question with you. The bell holds the time.
Spinoza. A philosopher raised in Amsterdam's Portuguese Jewish community, placed under a ban by its leaders, and argued about ever since. Today's word.
Your line: argued about ever since. Today, when someone disagrees with you, listen long enough to say their view back in words they'd accept. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

959.title: Readmitted to England
959.hook: Menasseh ben Israel petitions Cromwell, and Jews quietly return
959.howItsDone: Jewish communities in Britain trace their modern history to this quiet return, and the Spanish and Portuguese congregation in London still keeps the customs of the families who came back.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Spinoza, cut off by his community and argued about ever since. Did you manage to say someone else's view back to them fairly? Today the week ends, and a door that had been shut for a long time begins to open. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

A few weeks ago on this path, a king ordered every Jew out of England. Homes emptied. A London street kept only the name, Old Jewry. Now a rabbi from Amsterdam is crossing the North Sea with a petition in his bag. He is a teacher, a writer and a printer, and he has a big hope and a practical request. He wants to ask England's ruler, Oliver Cromwell, a simple question: may we come back? Today, what answer he got.
screen: `ENGLAND'S DOOR, SHUT.` → `A RABBI FROM AMSTERDAM.` → `MAY WE COME BACK?`

segments.voice: His name was Menasseh ben Israel. He came from the Amsterdam community we met two days ago, and he carried two kinds of reasons. One was a hope. The Torah speaks of Israel scattered from one end of the earth to the other, and Menasseh wrote that the redemption would come once the scattering was complete. If Jews could live in England too, he believed, that day would come nearer. The other reason was plainer: Jews needed places to live safely, and they could bring trade and skill. He addressed Cromwell in writing, and later answered the old lies about Jews in a pamphlet of his own. Cromwell called a conference in London. Merchants, lawyers and clergy argued. Some wanted Jews admitted. Some wanted strict conditions. Some wanted no admission at all. And the meeting ended without a formal decision. No law was passed. No grand gate swung open. Menasseh was left disappointed. But something quieter happened. A small group of Jews was already living in London, living outwardly as Spanish and Portuguese Catholic merchants. They asked to pray together in private and to bury their dead, and they were allowed to. They rented a house for a synagogue and found land for a cemetery. That is what readmitted looks like here: not a ceremony, but a door left unlocked, and people walking through it carefully. Look back over this week. A tablecloth spread over a code of law. The lion of Safed. Mystics walking out to greet Shabbat. Walls around the ghetto in Venice. A new home in Amsterdam. A son of that home cut off. And now, a door that had been shut opening a crack.

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: ask for a door to open. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Think of one door in your life that is closed: a relationship, a place, a chance you want. Menasseh asked in writing, plainly, and made his case. What would your request sound like if you said it plainly? Shape it in your mind in one or two sentences. You don't have to send it today. Just find the words. If you pray, you can bring that request in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Readmitted to England. Jews returning to the country that had expelled them, not by a grand law but by quiet permission to live, pray and bury their dead. Today's word.
Your line: readmitted. Today, if a door has opened a crack for you, walk through it, even carefully. Or open one a crack for someone else. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.
